interest: For historians, this file offers an exceptionally granular, multi-layered view of Japan’s rapid slide toward a totalitarian command structure and global conflict on the eve of the Pacific War. Beyond formal diplomatic exchanges—most notably Ambassador Grew's foundational September 1940 'green telegram' series advocating naval deterrence—the file is rich in candid internal intelligence, documenting fierce bureaucratic infighting (such as the Kobayashi–Kishi clash over wartime economic control), grassroots social regimentation, and popular sentiment captured in translated Bungei Shunju polls. It also illuminates rarely documented backchannel diplomacy and political vulnerabilities, including business opposition to the Axis alliance, clandestine peace proposals involving figures like M. Kleiman and Gracie Hall Roosevelt, rumors of an anti-war military coup led by General Ugaki, and the controversial circulation of Captain Bonner F. Fellers' 1935 study on the psychology of the Japanese soldier.
overview: This archival file (State Department decimal file 894.00, covering Japanese political affairs from late 1940 to 1942, part 1) provides comprehensive documentation of Japan’s internal political transformation and deteriorating foreign relations throughout 1940 and early 1941. Composed of diplomatic telegrams, embassy despatches, military and naval intelligence reports, and State Department memoranda, the file chronicles the fall of the Abe Cabinet, the brief tenure and military-engineered collapse of Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai's moderate government, and the consolidation of power under Prince Fumimaro Konoe's second cabinet. The collection details Japan's transition toward an authoritarian wartime regime through the dissolution of political parties, the creation of the totalitarian 'New National Structure' (Shintaisei) and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association (IRAA), and intense bureaucratic conflicts over state economic controls and rationing. Simultaneously, it records Japan's realignment toward the Axis via the Tripartite Pact, its proclamation of the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, and escalating friction with the United States, anchored by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's pivotal assessments advocating American firmness and naval deterrence.
